svg.title: Regional failover: share of new requests still sent to a failed region
svg.desc: Region A fails at 0 seconds. Health checks every 10 seconds with a failure threshold of 3 mark it unhealthy at about 30 seconds, and the authoritative DNS servers start answering with region B. Three curves show the share of new requests still reaching region A. With a global proxy or anycast entry point, new requests move as soon as the failure is detected, so the share falls from 100 percent to almost zero just after 30 seconds. With DNS and a 60-second TTL, resolvers keep their cached answer until it expires, so the share falls roughly linearly from 30 to 90 seconds, leaving a small tail of clients that cache longer or reuse open connections. With a 300-second TTL, the share falls from 30 to 330 seconds and about 10 percent of new requests still reach the failed region at 300 seconds. Failover time is detection plus cache expiry plus client behavior.

g.text: Share of new requests still reaching region A after it fails at 0 s
30 s: third failed check; DNS now answers with region B
Global proxy or anycast: new connections move as soon as the failure is detected
DNS with a 60 s TTL: cached answers expire by about 90 s, then a small tail of slow clients
DNS with a 300 s TTL: about 10% of new requests still reach region A at 300 s
Failover time = detection + cache expiry + client behavior; a global proxy removes the cache wait.
